findings: Right lung appears hyperinflated and hyperlucent relative to the left, with absent vascular markings in the right upper and mid zones, consistent with markedly reduced pulmonary vascularity on that side
A lobulated, partially calcified hilar/perihilar mass-like opacity is present at the right hilum, with dense central calcification in a popcorn or eggshell pattern
The left lung demonstrates diffusely increased interstitial markings with a reticular pattern throughout, most prominent in the lower and mid zones, with no frank consolidation
The left hemidiaphragm is slightly elevated and the cardiac silhouette appears shifted mildly toward the left
Bony thorax: ribs appear intact bilaterally; no gross lytic or sclerotic lesions identified
The right hemidiaphragm is well-defined and at a normal level
differential: Unilateral hyperlucent lung (right) due to large vessel obstruction or Swyer-James-MacLeod syndrome, with the right hilar calcified mass representing a calcified lymph node or carcinoid tumor causing proximal obstruction; left lung interstitial changes may represent reactive or inflammatory process

Right hilar calcified mass most consistent with a calcified granuloma (e.g., histoplasmosis or tuberculosis) with associated post-obstructive hyperinflation of right lung; left lung reticular pattern suggesting chronic interstitial lung disease (e.g., hypersensitivity pneumonitis or pulmonary fibrosis)

Right lung primary carcinoid tumor with calcification at the right hilum causing proximal bronchial obstruction and distal air trapping, with left lung showing superimposed pulmonary edema or lymphangitic carcinomatosis
anatomyConcerns: The right lung is markedly hyperlucent compared to the left, which is an asymmetric finding requiring correlation with clinical history and CT

The reticular pattern is confined to the left lung, which is an atypical lateralized distribution for most bilateral interstitial lung diseases and may suggest asymmetric disease or unilateral pathology
